theme: God’s sovereign election; Israel and the promise
readingInstruction: Read Romans 9:1-33. This chapter begins three chapters (9 to 11) on God’s purposes for Israel. Read it prayerfully, noting Paul’s sorrow, his focus on God’s mercy, and the question of who belongs to Israel.
settingTheScene: Romans 8 ended with the certainty that nothing can separate believers from God’s love. A Jewish reader might object: if God’s promises to Israel have failed, how can we trust his promises to us? Paul takes up this question in chapters 9 to 11. Chapter 9 explains that God’s word has not failed, because the promise always worked by election, not by physical descent. This chapter has been argued over for centuries, and it deserves careful and humble reading.
observation: “I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart” (9:2).
“To them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises” (9:4).
“But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel” (9:6).
“For he says to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (9:15).
“So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (9:16).
“But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” (9:20).
“Those who were not my people I will call my people, and her who was not beloved I will call beloved” (9:25).
“Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (9:33).
interpretation:
Paul begins with grief. “I am speaking the truth in Christ… I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers.” Like Moses, who asked to be blotted out for the sake of the people (Exodus 32:32), Paul loves his people so much that he would give up his own salvation if it could save them. This is the heart of a missionary. Any teaching of election that does not produce this kind of love has missed the point.

He lists Israel’s privileges: adoption, glory, covenants, the law, worship, promises, patriarchs, and “from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever.” This is one of the clearest statements of Christ’s deity.

Then the key claim: “It is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel.” The true Israel was always defined by God’s promise, not by physical descent. Isaac, not Ishmael. Jacob, not Esau, chosen “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad, in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls.” “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” a Hebrew idiom of preference, citing Malachi 1:2-3.

Paul anticipates the objection: “Is there injustice on God’s part? By no means!” He cites Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.” Salvation “depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.” Pharaoh is the example of one who was hardened, so that God’s power might be shown. The potter and the clay: “Who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” God has the right to show wrath and make known his power, and to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, “whom he has prepared beforehand for glory, even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles.”

Christians differ on how to read this chapter. Reformed interpreters see individual election to salvation: God sovereignly chooses those he will save. Others (Arminian and many other evangelicals) read the chapter as corporate election, focused on groups and on God’s purposes in history, or hold that God elects in view of foreseen faith. Everyone agrees on what Paul emphasizes: salvation is wholly by God’s mercy, and no one has a claim on him. And the chapter closes by returning to faith. Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained it by faith; Israel pursued it by works and stumbled over the stone. Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.

Do not use this chapter as a place to argue. Use it as a place to worship. If you are saved, it is because God had mercy on you.
connection: Genesis 21:12 and 25:23 are the stories of Isaac and Jacob. Exodus 9:16, 33:19 and 4 to 14 tell of Pharaoh and Moses. Malachi 1:2-3 is quoted in verse 13. Isaiah 29:16 and Jeremiah 18:1-6 are the potter and the clay. Hosea 1:10 and 2:23 are quoted in verses 25 to 26. Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16 speak of the stone. Ephesians 1:4-5 and 2:8-9 speak of choice and grace. 1 Peter 2:4-10 says Christ is the cornerstone. John 6:37-44 teaches that the Father draws people. 2 Peter 3:9 says God is patient, not wishing that any should perish.
application:
Let this chapter humble you rather than divide you. Thank God for his mercy to you, which you did not earn.

Pray for people of Jewish background, and for your friends who do not believe, with the kind of anguish Paul had.

Ask whether you question God’s right to rule. Where do you answer back?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that you were not beloved and he called you beloved.
Tell him what you cannot understand about his choosing, and trust him.
Ask him to make you humble.
